# Discussion

## Summary of Findings

We hypothesized that connectivity-informed methods would bring little benefit for localizing a source but would reconstruct the spatial pattern of activity more accurately, with a gain that grows as activity spreads beyond its onset (@sec-introduction). The results support this hypothesis in simulation and, preliminarily, in intracranial recordings. Consistent with the first part, wCSET brought no consistent localization benefit. In simulation (Study I), it localized the source more accurately than sLORETA and wMNE but less accurately than CSET and dSPM. In patients who underwent epilepsy surgery (Study II), no method localized the epileptogenic zone significantly better than wCSET, which was non-inferior to CSET and dSPM. Consistent with the second part, wCSET reconstructed the spatial pattern of activity more accurately than every other method throughout the simulated spike, and its advantage over the standard methods grew as activity spread, from Δr = `{python} corr1_std_dr_qrp_lo`–`{python} corr1_std_dr_qrp_hi` at 25% of the peak amplitude to `{python} corr1_std_dr_pp_lo`–`{python} corr1_std_dr_pp_hi` at the peak. Simultaneous intracranial recordings (Study III) showed the same advantage, arising mostly after the spike peak, in one of the two patients with cortical sources but not in the other.

These results suggest that localization alone is an incomplete benchmark for connectivity-informed methods. Localization did not consistently favor wCSET, whereas the spatial pattern of activity did, increasingly so as activity spread. A benchmark that measures only where a source lies and how far it extends at onset therefore misses where these priors should help most.

No single dataset is sufficient to measure this gain, either. Simulations are exact but rest on simplified models of the head, of the spread of activity and of noise. Resections are clinically grounded but spatially coarse, and intracranial recordings are direct but sparse. Because each has a different blind spot, results that agree across them carry more weight than any one alone. Here, simulation and surgery agree that wCSET brings no consistent localization advantage, and simulation and one intracranial patient agree on its advantage in the spatial pattern of activity.

The surrogate and perturbation analyses address a practical question: whether wCSET needs an individual connectome. In simulation, it did not. With the atlas and local surrogates, which require no diffusion MRI, wCSET's localization was non-inferior to that with the individual connectome used to generate the data, and its spatial correlation fell by only Δr = `{python} surr_match_pp_lo`–`{python} surr_match_pp_hi`. Its advantage in spatial correlation also survived perturbation of up to `{python} deg_corr_wcset_better_end`% of the connectome's edges. Replacing the connectome with cortical geometry, however, mattered in simulation. GBF localized significantly worse, and the loss that CSET showed with geometric harmonics suggests that the harmonics, rather than GBF's weights, cause GBF's loss. In the clinical data, GBF and wCSET performed similarly: neither localized the epileptogenic zone significantly better than the other (Study II), and they reached similar correlations in Patient 1 (Study III). We discuss this discrepancy further in @sec-connectome-geometry.

## Localization

As expected, wCSET brought no consistent localization benefit: it was less accurate than CSET and dSPM in simulation but showed no detectable disadvantage in patients.

At 25% of the peak amplitude, wCSET localized the simulated source more accurately than sLORETA and wMNE, but less accurately than CSET and dSPM, by `{python} loc1_cset_hl` and `{python} loc1_dspm_hl`. It was not shown to be non-inferior to either. A connectivity prior has little to add at that point, while activity is still confined to the initial patch, so we expected no advantage there. The disadvantage reflects bimodal errors. wCSET placed its peak inside the initial patch more often than CSET and dSPM (`{python} loc1_exact_wcset`% of runs against `{python} loc1_exact_cset`% and `{python} loc1_exact_dspm`%), but it also placed it more than 30 mm away more often (`{python} loc1_far_wcset`% against `{python} loc1_far_cset`% and `{python} loc1_far_dspm`%). This disadvantage depends on noise: at higher SNR, wCSET localized more accurately than dSPM (@sec-s1-data-noise).

Study II also showed no consistent advantage. No method localized the epileptogenic zone significantly better than wCSET, although the point estimates favored wCSET by `{python} resection_hl_lo` to `{python} resection_hl_hi` mm. wCSET was non-inferior to CSET and dSPM within the `{python} resection_margin` mm margin, so it localized no more than `{python} resection_margin` mm worse than either. Against GBF, sLORETA and wMNE, the `{python} resection_ci_pct`% CIs were too wide to rule out a larger disadvantage. With `{python} resection_n` patients, Study II could detect only large differences in localization error, not differences as small as those found in simulation, and it leaves open disadvantages of up to `{python} resection_open_worse` mm and advantages of up to `{python} resection_open_better` mm. The proportion of patients whose resection volume contained the peak gave the same picture. `{python} resection_inside_lead` placed the peak inside it in `{python} resection_inside_top`, more often than any other method. Only dSPM, which placed the peak inside it in none, did significantly worse than wCSET.

Localization was less accurate in patients than in simulation. In simulation, wCSET's peak lay a median of `{python} simf_loc_trial_median_wcset` mm from the initial patch. Since a resection volume is a much larger target than an initial patch, one would expect wCSET's peak to fall inside it in nearly every patient. It did so in only `{python} resection_inside_wcset` of `{python} resection_n`. Several differences between real recordings and our simulation may explain this gap. Real physiological noise is probably larger than our noise model assumes, and Study II could be whitened only with a diagonal noise covariance (@sec-data-resection). The target itself may be imperfect: interictal spikes arise from the irritative zone, which can extend beyond the epileptogenic zone and therefore beyond the resection [@rosenow_presurgical_2001]. Finally, by 50% of the peak amplitude, the spike may already include activity that has propagated from its origin.

On the same cohort, @wang_geometry_2026 found no significant difference between GBF and dSPM, sLORETA or eLORETA (p = 0.079–0.133), consistent with our results. They did find GBF more accurate than depth-weighted MNE (p = 0.012), whereas wCSET did not differ significantly from our wMNE, possibly because our wMNE uses a different depth weighting and regularization (@sec-inverse).

Study II still answered the question it was included for. Localization against a resection is the field's conventional benchmark. On it, no method significantly outperformed wCSET, and wCSET was non-inferior to CSET and dSPM. In patients, its advantage in the spatial pattern of activity therefore came at no detectable cost in localization.

## Spatial Pattern of Activity

wCSET's advantage in the spatial pattern of activity appeared before activity spread, grew as it spread, withstood noise and connectome errors, and was partly reproduced in intracranial recordings.

In simulation, wCSET's spatial correlation with the simulated activity was higher than that of every other method from onset until `{python} corr1_window_end_lo`–`{python} corr1_window_end_hi` ms. Its advantage over the standard methods was already present at 25% of the peak amplitude (Δr = `{python} corr1_std_dr_qrp_lo`–`{python} corr1_std_dr_qrp_hi`), while activity was still confined to the initial patch. Spread beyond the patch therefore cannot explain this early advantage, but local connectivity can. The dipoles of the patch are linked by the short-range edges that every connectome in this study contains (@sec-connectome), so the prior favors activity that covers the patch as a whole. Previous studies found that priors built on connectome or geometric harmonics reconstruct the spatial extent of a source more accurately than standard methods [@siu_structural_2026; @wang_geometry_2026]. Such a better-delimited source, with less spurious activity elsewhere on the cortex, would explain the higher whole-cortex correlation before activity spreads. The advantage then grew as activity spread beyond the patch, reaching Δr = `{python} corr1_std_dr_pp_lo`–`{python} corr1_std_dr_pp_hi` at the peak.

The connectome spectrum may help explain why the advantage grew. This spectrum describes activity as a combination of connectome harmonics, from low-frequency patterns that vary smoothly across connected regions to high-frequency patterns that vary rapidly (@sec-connectome). @rue-queralt_connectome_2021 computed it for source-reconstructed visual evoked responses and found that it became more compact as the response rose: a few harmonics, mostly of low frequency, captured most of the signal. This observation motivates connectome-based priors. CSET's sparse prior favors a few harmonics, and wCSET's weights additionally favor the low-frequency ones. If activity likewise becomes more compact in the connectome spectrum as it spreads, these priors should fit it increasingly well, and their advantage should grow with spread, as it did here. The low-frequency weights may also explain why wCSET's advantage exceeded CSET's.

This advantage was robust. wCSET's spatial correlation remained higher than that of the standard methods down to an SNR of `{python} noise_corr_end_std`. It also withstood errors in the connectome, which matters because real tractography contains many false-positive connections [@maier-hein_challenge_2017]. With up to `{python} deg_corr_wcset_better_end`% of edges swapped, wCSET's spatial correlation remained higher than sLORETA's and dSPM's; CSET's did so with up to `{python} deg_corr_cset_better_end`% swapped. Localization was more sensitive: wCSET became less accurate than sLORETA once `{python} deg_loc_wcset_sloreta_worse_start`% of edges were swapped, and CSET once `{python} deg_loc_cset_sloreta_worse_start`% were. With most edges swapped, the connectome no longer indicates which regions are connected, so the prior misleads the reconstruction. Both methods then performed worse than sLORETA and dSPM in spatial correlation (Δr = `{python} deg_corr_worse_dr_all`) and worse than sLORETA in localization (by `{python} deg_loc_worse_sloreta_mm` mm).

Simultaneous intracranial recordings partly support these simulation results. Only two of the four patients had cortical sources (the other two are discussed in @sec-limitations), so the recordings offer a proof of concept rather than a validation. wCSET's advantage appeared in Patient 1 but not in Patient 2. In Patient 1, wCSET's virtual iEEG correlated with the recording at r = `{python} signed_48_wcset` over the comparison window, whereas the standard methods' did not (r = `{python} signed_48_std_lo` to `{python} signed_48_std_hi`). wCSET outperformed them and CSET, mostly after the spike peak. This timing is consistent with the simulation, in which the advantage grew as activity spread. In Patient 2, the standard methods reached r = `{python} signed_34_std_lo`–`{python} signed_34_std_hi` and wCSET only `{python} signed_34_wcset`. This difference was not significant (p_corrected ≥ `{python} signed_34_p_min[2:]`), but it went against wCSET. In both patients, GBF reached a correlation similar to wCSET's.

Absolute agreement with the recording was modest in both patients. wCSET's correlation over the comparison window reached r = `{python} signed_48_wcset` in Patient 1 and `{python} signed_34_wcset` in Patient 2. @afnan_assessing_2026 report correlations of 0.14–0.45 between MEG and simultaneous SEEG at the spike peak. A window average includes samples of lower SNR than the peak and would be expected to fall below a peak value, so our correlations appear in line with this benchmark. Agreement of this size may therefore be inherent to comparisons with intracranial recordings rather than specific to EEG or to our methods. Sparse sampling likely contributes: even with 67 to 146 contacts per patient, the electrodes sample only a small fraction of the cortex on which activity is reconstructed. Larger cohorts will be needed to tell whether Patient 1 or Patient 2 is the more typical case.

## Connectome or Geometry? {#sec-connectome-geometry}

wCSET did not need the individual connectome. In simulation, with the atlas and both local surrogates, wCSET's localization and spatial correlation stayed within the non-inferiority margins of those with the individual connectome, even though the simulated activity spread along the individual connectome itself. The largest disadvantages that the CIs allowed were `{python} surr_match_loc_ci` mm in localization and Δr = `{python} surr_match_pp_ci` in spatial correlation. A surrogate is therefore a practical option when diffusion MRI is unavailable, as is usually the case in clinical epilepsy workups, and Studies II and III used the atlas surrogate for this reason.

Two surrogates fell short in localization. GBF localized `{python} surr_beltrami_loc_d` mm worse than wCSET with the individual connectome (`{python} surr_ci_pct`% CI `{python} surr_beltrami_loc_lo` to `{python} surr_beltrami_loc_hi` mm worse), and wCSET with the binarized atlas localized `{python} surr_atlasbin_loc_d` mm worse (`{python} surr_ci_pct`% CI from `{python} surr_atlasbin_loc_better` mm better to `{python} surr_atlasbin_loc_worse` mm worse). Neither CI ruled out a disadvantage beyond the `{python} loc1_delta` mm margin. GBF also lowered the spatial correlation at the peak, but only by Δr = `{python} surr_beltrami_pp`, well within the `{python} DELTA_CORR` margin. CSET showed the same pattern more strongly: geometric harmonics worsened its localization by `{python} cset_beltrami_loc_d` mm (`{python} surr_ci_pct`% CI `{python} cset_beltrami_loc_lo` to `{python} cset_beltrami_loc_hi` mm), whereas the other surrogates changed it by at most `{python} cset_other_loc_max` mm. Because CSET uses no harmonic weights, this comparison changes only the harmonics, which points to the harmonics, rather than GBF's weights, as the cause of GBF's loss.

In patients, these disadvantages were not detected. For spatial correlation, this is expected. In Study III, GBF's correlation did not differ significantly from wCSET's in either patient with cortical sources. The disadvantage in simulation (Δr = `{python} surr_beltrami_pp_d`) is too small for the bootstrap within a single patient to resolve: in Patient 1, the `{python} surr_ci_pct`% CI of the difference was `{python} signed_48_beltrami_ci_width` wide. For localization, the absence of a difference is less informative. In Study II, wCSET localized better than GBF by `{python} resection_gbf_d` mm, in the same direction as in simulation, but the `{python} resection_ci_pct`% CI ranged from `{python} resection_gbf_worse` mm worse to `{python} resection_gbf_better` mm better. With `{python} resection_n` patients and the resection as a coarse reference, Study II could not detect a difference of the size seen in simulation. @siu_structural_2026, who used the harmonics to filter source reconstructions rather than as a prior, also found that geometric and connectome harmonics performed similarly against resected epileptogenic zones in 20 patients.

The connectome still has to reflect how the cortex is organized. With most edges swapped at random, wCSET performed worse than sLORETA and dSPM in spatial correlation and worse than sLORETA in localization (@sec-s1-prior-noise). The surrogates, however, are far from random. In terms of how closely their priors match the individual prior, every surrogate, including GBF, is equivalent to swapping only `{python} deg_surr_equiv_lo`–`{python} deg_surr_equiv_hi`% of the edges (@sec-s1-prior-noise). Since wCSET kept its correlation advantage with up to `{python} deg_corr_wcset_better_end`% of edges swapped, every surrogate should preserve that advantage, as all of them did. This measure does not, however, explain GBF's localization disadvantage, because GBF's prior is nearly as close to the individual prior as those of the other surrogates. What in geometric harmonics impairs localization in simulation remains open.

Connectome or geometry? For the spatial pattern of activity, either supports wCSET's advantage, and an atlas connectome is enough. For localization, connectome harmonics did better in simulation, a difference that our clinical cohorts were too small to confirm or rule out.

## Limitations {#sec-limitations}

The strongest evidence for wCSET's advantage comes from simulation, in which activity spreads along the connectome. This design builds in the assumption on which connectome-based priors rest: that activity spreading along the connectome has a compact connectome spectrum. The assumption is grounded in data: @rue-queralt_connectome_2021 found such compact spectra in source-reconstructed evoked responses. It is also as defensible as the independent focal sources of most simulations, which match the assumptions of the standard methods. If real activity follows the connectome less closely, however, wCSET's advantage would likely be smaller than in simulation. Perturbing the connectome used for reconstruction shows that the advantage does not require an exact match (@sec-s1-prior-noise), and the clinical studies, though small, offer a partial test in real data.

How activity spreads is also simplified: it propagates hop by hop, without feedback. Neural mass models include feedback, but at the resolution of our source space, our attempts produced either a focal spike or a full seizure, and nothing in between. Coarser models with about 1,000 nodes are stable, but too coarse for EEG source modeling. A patch of cortex can be modeled as a single dipole only if its extent is much smaller than its distance to the scalp, which requires sources less than about 5 mm apart [@nunez_multi-scale_2019, p. 199]. Our source space meets this criterion with a spacing of 3.3 mm (@sec-source-space), whereas 1,000-node models space their nodes about 10 mm apart [@siu_structural_2026]. Whole-brain neural mass models at dipole resolution remain a step for future work.

The source model has a limitation of its own: it restricts dipoles to the cortex (@sec-source-space), so it cannot represent deep generators. In the two Study III patients with deep sources, no method's virtual iEEG agreed with the recording, a limitation that @grova_intracranial_2016 also report. Excluding deep structures is a missed opportunity, because tractography, the very data our prior draws on, also captures connections to and among them. Including them is not straightforward, however. On the cortex, each source can be oriented perpendicular to the surface, but deep structures offer no such surface, so their sources need free orientations. It is unclear what a connection between two differently oriented sources would mean, so the connectome would have to encode orientation as well.

Finally, CSET's regularization parameter was fixed at a single value, tuned in simulation, because the SNR rule we used for the other methods applies only to Gaussian priors (@sec-lambda). A fixed value cannot adapt to the SNR of each recording, which may have disadvantaged CSET in real data.

# Conclusion

Source reconstruction is conventionally benchmarked on the location and extent of a single, focal generator, a criterion that says little about how well a method reconstructs the spatial pattern of activity as it spreads across distributed regions. We introduced wCSET, which replaces CSET's sparse prior with a Gaussian prior on the connectome spectrum whose weights decay exponentially with graph frequency. We validated it alongside CSET, three standard methods and a geometry-based alternative (GBF) against three references: a simulation of activity spreading along the structural connectome, the resected epileptogenic zone of seizure-free patients, and simultaneous intracranial recordings.

wCSET brought no consistent localization benefit: in simulation, it localized more accurately than sLORETA and wMNE but less accurately than CSET and dSPM, and in the resection cohort, no method localized significantly better than it. wCSET did, however, reconstruct the spatial pattern of activity more accurately than every other method throughout the simulated spike, with an advantage that grew as activity spread and withstood noise and large connectome errors. Intracranial recordings showed the same advantage in one of the two patients with cortical sources. In simulation, atlas and local surrogate connectomes preserved this advantage, so wCSET need not rely on individual diffusion MRI. GBF, built on geometric harmonics, preserved it too, but localized less accurately in simulation. Connectivity-informed priors thus pay off in the spatial pattern of activity rather than in localization, a gain that benchmarks of localization alone cannot detect.

Beyond wCSET itself, we see the three-part validation framework as the more lasting contribution: simulated, surgical and intracranial references that together probe a source's spatial pattern of activity, not only its location. Its simulation, in which activity spreads along the structural connectome at dipole resolution, is openly available, and its intracranial comparison applies to any simultaneous EEG–iEEG dataset (@sec-data-availability). Natural next steps are to apply this framework to future connectivity- and geometry-informed methods, and to extend it to source models that include deep generators and to larger intracranial cohorts. These steps would help source imaging reconstruct not only where activity begins, but how it unfolds across the brain’s network, a prerequisite for studying how its regions interact.
